title: Multipartite synchronization residuals in driven-dissipative spin networks
authors: Jatin Ghildiyal, Shubhrangshu Dasgupta, Asoka Biswas
abstract: We introduce a phase-space measure of quantum synchronization that quantifies relative phase localization for two-qubit and three-qubit systems. This measure is built from the first angular moments of phase distributions obtained from Husimi-Q quasiprobability functions. Using this framework, we formulate a new class of synchronization residuals, motivated by subadditivity-type hierarchies of information-theoretic measures. We investigate these residuals in a driven-dissipative quantum Rabi network in the dispersive adiabatic regime. We show that, for two qubits, collective synchronization remains bounded by single-qubit contributions yielding a non-negative bipartite residual. The three-qubit nonequilibrium steady state exhibits a negative tripartite residual, which indicates collective phase synchronization, which cannot be described by pairwise decomposition. The corresponding entropy-based residuals, however, remain non-negative in both cases. Our results therefore, underscore that phase-sensitive synchronization measures and entropic correlation measures probe distinct aspects of open-system dynamics.
summary: The paper develops phase-space measures to quantify quantum synchronization in driven-dissipative spin networks. By analyzing the resulting residuals for two and three qubits, the authors demonstrate a key distinction: phase-sensitive measures can reveal collective locking (negative residual) that is not captured by standard entropic correlation measures. This highlights that different mathematical tools probe distinct physical aspects of open system dynamics.
main_problem: The central problem is quantifying multipartite quantum synchronization, specifically determining if collective phase coherence can be fully described by summing up pairwise contributions.
main_result: For three qubits in a driven-dissipative network, the phase-space derived tripartite residual becomes negative, indicating genuine collective locking beyond pairwise description, while entropy-based residuals remain non-negative.
method: The authors introduce and analyze novel synchronization residuals built from first angular moments of phase distributions obtained via Husimi-Q quasiprobability functions in the phase space.
model_or_system: The study uses a driven-dissipative quantum Rabi network involving two or three qubits coupled to cavity modes. The analysis is performed in the dispersive adiabatic regime, leading to effective qubit Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Phase-space synchronization residuals ($\Delta^{(3)}_R$), bipartite residual ($\Delta^{(2)}_R$), and corresponding entropy-based residuals ($\Delta^{(3)}_S$).
important_parameters: Dispersive adiabatic regime; two-qubit and three-qubit coupling strengths ($J_{ij}$); cavity detunings ($\Delta_c, \Delta_i$); decay rates ($\gamma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on using Husimi-Q quasiprobability distributions to approximate the true phase distributions in open quantum systems.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates two qubits coupled to a cavity system, while other figures likely compare different residual types or show time evolution of synchronization measures.
paper_structure: The paper develops theoretical bounds (analogous to subadditivity/strong subadditivity) for multi-partite coherence measures. It calculates these residuals for 2 and 3 qubits in a specific physical model, comparing the results derived from phase-space moments versus entropy correlations.
why_interesting: This work provides a sophisticated diagnostic tool—the synchronization residual—to distinguish between genuine multipartite quantum correlations (which violate simple additive bounds) and those that can be decomposed into pairwise interactions within open quantum systems dynamics.

Figure 3c shows the steady-state synchronization resid- ual ∆(2) R (t) as a function of the intercavity hopping am- plitude J12. In an otherwise monotonically decreasing profile, one sees a sharp feature at J12 ∼∆c = 5. This is an artefact of a singularity at J12 = ∆c of the adiabatic Hamiltonian, that leads to a level crossing as can be seen from the variation of its eigenvalues with J12 (see Fig. 3d).
